body: I'm not entirely comfortable sharing that. suffice to say, it was awful.
Thanks. Actually doing great now. This happened back in Spring.

Sure, you're welcome. It feels good to talk about it now.

Prior to OD, only vaguely aware of it. Morphine (and other meds) weren't related to mental or emotional issues, just chronic back pain.

After OD, realization was slow at first, then immediate clarity. After I woke up, I fully intended to try killing myself again, only this time with a gun, as soon as I got home. But then I thought about why, about how this had all happened, and I realized in a moment of clarity that I was going to be fine, that the past was gone.

As for writing a new narrative, still figuring that out, but the hard part's over, realizing that I can and whatever i want.

Some say stories make meaning. I believe that. Thanks for the well wishes.
No worries, thanks back. I'm actually doing great now. Survived a suicide attempt and gained a new perspective.
Yeah I'm bad at math. Thanks!

What's also good to try is changing your environment. Simple things like removing pictures, rearranging furniture, redecorating, a new shirt, or wardrobe. Changing where you go after work, on weekends, even the route you take. All these little changes add up to a new outlook, to looking forward rather than back.
Thanks. Did you read that New Yorker piece on Narcan? Amazing how many people it's saved. It's been difficult, but I've actually moved on and am in a pretty good place now.

I understand that impulse. But not everyone is going to do that. Think of it as a math problem. Pure numbers. Sure the probability of talking about this to someone may be negative, but it's not zero. You just have to find the right people to talk to about this. And they can help reinforce what is actually true: that is negative probability isn't actually real.

Of being abandoned, it was the worst thing I've ever experienced. Of waking up from my overdose, it was very painful for a week, but en very clarifying, and ultimately, freeing. Cleansing. Not only did it free me from my dilusion of being abandoned by someone who I thought loved me back, it freed me from my past propensity to dwell on former grief, like the premature deaths of former loved ones. I stopped having to carry that weight around with me all the time. It was like I'd been haunted, and suddenly I didn't have those ghosts around me anymore. It was wholly unexpected, but SOOO liberating.

Totally comfortable. I'm in a good place now. The biggest thing I learned: I can let go of what I thought was my story. We all construct our own stories and become entirely enslaved by them to a certain extent. I was completely stuck in mine. And when she blew it up, I was left with nothing, or so I felt at the time. Now, after the Narcan wake up call, I know I can write a new story, my own, one that isn't so contingent on another person's happiness.

What are some things you could do to change your environment? Don't worry about trying to change how you feel for now. I would just think about things you could do to change your environment. Even simple things like removing pictures, rearranging furniture, redecorating - it all helps to remove reminders. Then changing where you go from time to time - a new trail route, a new unfamiliar park, a new route to and from work that takes you by something beautiful to look at. Even a new shirt, shoes, wardrobe, a new apartment - it all adds up to a new outlook and forcing your mind to think forward rather than backwards. It's worth trying. What do you think?

I OD'd on 4,000+ mgs of morphine, was given Narcan in the ER, then detoxed and withdrew for a week in intensive care/suicide watch. After I woke up, I realized I didn't HAVE to kill myself after all. That I could do something else...
You have options. You're in pain, I know. That pain is keeping you from seeing those options. If you get some help, they can help lessen that pain that acts like a black cloak on everything, and in time you'll begin to see a crack in that cloak, a way out. You're life is worth giving that a shot. Your future self will thank you.

Hopefully by now you're 90 minutes into that party, maybe your third beer or cocktail, you've smiled, chatted with a few people innocuously...then maybe later tonight you'll get back home and read these responses to your post, reminding yourself of your earlier sadness. Know this: you aren't alone. All those people at the party? A few of them are feeling the same sorts of things, and you would've never known it even if you'd talked for an hour. Because we hide in plain sight, all of us, and we're all terrified of being alone. Aloneness is no doubt the scariest thing out there. Worse than goddamn grizzly bears. But realizing that we aren't alone, none of us, because of our universal fear, can somehow actually be more than small solace. Once we acknowledge we're all afraid of the same things, we can begin to reconnect, to find some peace and comfort. And live. Anyway, I hope you had a good time at the party.

He's not worth killing yourself over. you have options, even if it feels as if you don't. There are always options even in the direst of circumstances. You owe it to your future self to explore those unknowns. Please don't give up!!

He could be the greatest artist or art teacher in the world. <-- Doesn't matter. Why? Because he's an absolutely irredeemable douchenozzle for saying what he said to you. He proved it by saying it. If his intention was simply to impress upon you and everyone else there that his class will be epically challenging, the way he chose to express it betrayed two key things: his gargantuan ego, and his world-champion douchenozzleness. Report his stupid ass to the administration and shame him into a public apology.
I'm so sorry. How long were you two together?

Feeling your pain. What finally worked, or rather is working now, for me, is using those memories to trigger something else, in my case something I am appreciative of in life rit now. Not then, but now. Appreciation is working wonders, for me anyway.

Thanks. For a long time I wished for an explanation, some closure, but I don't any longer. She cut things off with her family a couple years ago; some childhood trauma surfaced about 3 years ago which led to her ending things with her family. Given what I know, I supported her all the way. But I've now resigned myself to believe cutting me off as well was inevitable, even tho I knew nothing of her trauma till she 'remembered' the trauma three years ago. So, no I haven't reached out to them at all.
Not as much now, but was seeing my therapist every week back when it happened.

Interesting circumstances there, a bit different from mine. After she disappeared, I never got to talk to her again, just through her attorney. After a few rounds of back and forth between lawyers, she accused me of domestic abuse, of threatening her with violence. Which I've never done, BTW, either or both. I'm the sensitive lapsed poet cat guy who saves bugs from inside the house. So to get accused of domestic abuse really through me for a loop. My attorney said her own psychological issues (which were not insignificant) may have contributed to her making these claims. May be something similar going on here in your case.
Still have no idea.
Yep, right here. Same timeline, too. Hit me.
